candidates.context: The liver is a major organ involved in the elimination of drugs through metabolism and/or biliary 42 excretion of unchanged drugs or their metabolites. Liver disease can change these metabolic and 43 excretory pathways by impacting drug metabolizing enzymes and transporters. 4 , 5 In addition, the 44 absorption and distribution of drugs can also be affected by liver disease. The presence and 45 magnitude of portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis can further affect a drug’s 46 pharmacokinetics to varying degrees because of alterations in hepatic arterial and portal blood 47 flow as well as intra- and extra-hepatic shunting. Portal hypertension can also affect systemic 48 circulation, leading to changes in the volume of distribution of a drug. candidates.statement: Other scoring systems using laboratory tests to assess the severity of liver disease exist, e.g., the 200 Model of End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score and the Albumin-Bilirubin (ALBI) score. 201 However, these scoring systems have not been sufficiently characterized with respect to their 202 ability to predict changes in pharmacokinetics to support their use in lieu of the CP score. When 203 using the CP classification, MELD scores can be useful for further stratification of disease 204 severity within CP groups B and C. Generally, when alternative scores are used, the CP 205 classification should also be assessed, and results should be reported for all classification 206 methods. FDA encourages assessment of other relevant markers to explore correlation with 207 pharmacokinetic change. 208

candidates.statement: Dosage recommendations in patients with HI should be based on the overall understanding of the 406 relationship between hepatic function, drug exposure, and the exposure-response relationships 407 for efficacy and safety. For drugs where small changes in exposure do not lead to clinically 408 significant differences in the safety and effectiveness of the drug, the recommended dosage of 409 the drug in patients with HI may be the same as in patients with normal hepatic function. When 410 there is a need for a different recommended dosage in patients with HI compared to those with 411 normal hepatic function, the dosage recommendations should be based on exposure-matching to 412 a reference group with an acceptable benefit-risk profile, often the normal hepatic function 413 group. 414
